newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Few Palestinian tears for sellers of the homeland.
newsitem.headline: Few Palestinian tears for sellers of the homeland.

text.p: A pair of West Bank killings which followed a Palestinian Authority ban on land sales to Jews have whipped up a storm of outrage in Israel and overseas but are just a tempest in a teacup for most Palestinians.

Locked in a century of struggle with Jews over the sliver of land between the Mediterranean Sea and Jordan River, Palestinians have little sympathy for those accused of selling off the homeland to the enemy.
"One who sells the land would sell his body," Faraj Abdel Latif, a 60-year-old produce vendor from the Balata refugee camp near Nablus in the West Bank, told Reuters.

"Anyone who takes part in these dirty activities is an outcast and a traitor and deserves the most severe punishment," said Abdel Latif, whose family fled the port city of Jaffa, now in Israel, after the Jewish state's independence in 1948.
Palestinian land dealers Farid Bashiti, 70, and Harbi Abu Salah, in his 60s, were found dead this month in PLO-ruled Ramallah within 10 days of each other.
Their killings came on the heels of a Palestinian Authority announcement that an old Jordanian law setting the death penalty for those who sold land to Israelis held sway in the West Bank.
Israel was quick to tie the land sales ban to the killings, now subject to separate Israeli and Palestinian investigations.
The PLO has denied any link to the two deaths but defends the ban as a necessary measure to combat the spread of Jewish settlements in occupied lands it wants for a future state.

The U.S.-based Human Rights Watch said it understood the PLO's concerns that private land purchases by Israelis would be used by Israel to lay claim to disputed areas, but said imposing the death penalty for such sales violated internationally accepted norms of human rights.
The U.S. State Department condemned the killings and urged the Palestinian Authority to apply the rule of law.
With PLO-Israel peace talks in paralysis and Palestinian rage boiling over the thorny issue of Jewish settlement in lands captured by Israel in 1967, most Palestinians shrug off the criticism.

"Severe punishment for those who sell land to Israelis is a step in the right direction but it came too late because no one knows how many houses and lands were sold in previous years." East Jerusalem merchant Husni Hamdan Abdelrahim told Reuters.

Real estate agents who hawk lands to Jews are condemned in the West Bank and Gaza as collaborators. Stories abound of unsavoury land dealers who prey on poor and indebted farmers to coerce them into parting with their property.

Giving religious sanction to the ban on land sales, Jerusalem's top Moslem cleric Mufti Ikrima Sabri gave renewed backing this month to a 70-year-old religious ruling barring Moslems who sold land to Jews being buried in a Moslem cemetery.

Some Palestinians say long prison terms are punishment enough for unscrupulous land agents but others, deeply bitter their hopes for a coveted state are vanishing as they see Israel steadily gobbling up the West Bank, demand sharper retribution.
"Selling land is a big treason," Riyad al-Fara, a 44-year-old contractor from the Gaza city of Khan Younis, told Reuters. "Anybody who sells any centimetre should be killed."
